title: Pointwise exponential of a locally nilpotent Lie derivation
statement:
Let $L$ be a Lie algebra over $\mathbf Q$ [def-wf-lie-algebra], of arbitrary dimension. Let $D:L\to L$ be a $\mathbf Q$-linear map satisfying
$$D([x,y])=[D(x),y]+[x,D(y)]\qquad(x,y\in L).$$
Assume $D$ is locally nilpotent, meaning that for every $x\in L$ there is an integer $N\geq1$ with $D^N(x)=0$. Here $D^0$ is the identity and $D^n$ denotes $n$-fold composition. The formula
$$\operatorname{Exp}_D(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\frac{D^n(x)}{n!}\quad\text{for any }N\geq1\text{ with }D^N(x)=0$$
is independent of $N$ and defines a $\mathbf Q$-linear Lie algebra automorphism of $L$, that is, a bijective linear map preserving the bracket. Its inverse is $\operatorname{Exp}_{-D}$, defined by the same pointwise finite-sum formula for $-D$.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, first proof, printed pp.503-504, Lie-theoretic input to the Serre presentation; characteristic-zero applicability on p.508. This pointwise exponential lemma is an agent-supplied prerequisite, not a theorem stated by Milne. WANTED: Serre, Complex Semisimple Lie Algebras, Chapter VI appendix, reflection construction.

proof.text: If $D^N x=0$, then $D^{N+j}x=D^j(0)=0$ for all $j\geq0$. Thus any two allowed cutoffs give the same sum after extending both to their maximum. For $a,b\in\mathbf Q$ and $x,y\in L$, choose a common cutoff $N$ annihilating both $x$ and $y$; it also annihilates $ax+by$. The finite sum of the linear maps $D^n/n!$ at this cutoff gives $\operatorname{Exp}_D(ax+by)=a\operatorname{Exp}_D(x)+b\operatorname{Exp}_D(y)$. Also $(-D)^n x=(-1)^nD^n x$, by induction, so $-D$ is locally nilpotent and the same construction gives a linear map $\operatorname{Exp}_{-D}$.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, first proof, printed pp.503-504, and characteristic-zero extension p.508: agent-supplied pointwise exponential prerequisite, not a theorem stated there.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-lie-derivation-iterate-binomial] to the given derivation: for every $n$, $D^n[x,y]=\sum_{i=0}^n\binom ni[D^i x,D^{n-i}y]$. Choose $r,s\geq1$ with $D^r x=0$ and $D^s y=0$. In the formula for $n=r+s$, each term has $i\geq r$ or $n-i\geq s$, and hence is zero. Consequently $D^{r+s}[x,y]=0$, an allowed cutoff for the bracket.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, first proof, printed pp.503-504, and characteristic-zero extension p.508: agent-supplied pointwise exponential prerequisite, not a theorem stated there.

proof.text:
Use cutoff $r+s$ on $[x,y]$ and substitute the formula from step 2. Since $\binom ni/n!=1/(i!(n-i)!)$ in $\mathbf Q$, reindex the finite sum by $j=n-i$. Terms with $i\geq r$ or $j\geq s$ vanish. Conversely every pair $0\leq i<r$, $0\leq j<s$ has $i+j<r+s$, so occurs exactly once. Thus
$$\operatorname{Exp}_D[x,y]=\sum_{i<r,j<s}\frac{[D^i x,D^j y]}{i!j!}=[\operatorname{Exp}_D x,\operatorname{Exp}_D y].$$
The last equality is precisely bilinearity of the bracket from [def-wf-lie-algebra].

source.place: Theorem 23.63, first proof, printed pp.503-504, and characteristic-zero extension p.508: agent-supplied pointwise exponential prerequisite, not a theorem stated there.

proof.text:
For $x$ choose $N\geq1$ with $D^N x=0$. Linearity and composition of powers give $D^N(\operatorname{Exp}_{\pm D}x)=\sum_{j<N}(\pm1)^jD^{N+j}x/j!=0$. Hence cutoff $N$ is valid for both outer maps when computing either composite at $x$. Expanding the finite sums gives
$$\operatorname{Exp}_{-D}(\operatorname{Exp}_D x)=\sum_{i,j<N}\frac{(-1)^i}{i!j!}D^{i+j}x.$$
Terms of total degree $k\geq N$ are zero. For $k<N$, all pairs $i+j=k$ occur, with coefficient $\frac1{k!}\sum_{i=0}^k\binom ki(-1)^i$. For $k>0$ this is $(1+(-1))^k/k!=0$ by [lem-pur-commutative-ring-binomial-expansion] over $\mathbf Q$; for $k=0$ the sum has the single coefficient $1$. The composite therefore equals $x$. For the reversed composite the coefficient is $\frac1{k!}\sum_{j=0}^k\binom kj(-1)^j$, giving the same result. These two identities prove bijectivity with inverse $\operatorname{Exp}_{-D}$. Together with linearity and step 3 this proves the claimed Lie algebra automorphism.
